Purpose: Define a brand's market position in one sentence
Structure: For [audience] / who [need] / our [product] is [category] / that [key benefit] / unlike [competitor]
When to Use: Launching a product or entering a new market
Example Skeleton: For [busy professionals] who [need to stay focused], [AppX] is a [productivity tool] that [blocks distractions] unlike [generic timers]
Strengths: Forces clarity on differentiation; aligns teams
Risks: Can sound corporate if overused externally

Purpose: Map product value to customer jobs and pains
When to Use: Early product-market fit work or repositioning
Example Skeleton: We help [segment] do [job] by [feature], relieving [pain] and creating [gain]
Strengths: Rooted in customer evidence; exposes gaps
Risks: Requires real research; risk of feature-focus over story

Purpose: Organize all brand claims into a coherent hierarchy
Structure: Roof (headline claim) + 3-4 Pillars (supporting proofs) + Foundation (brand purpose/values)
When to Use: Multi-audience comms planning; keeping teams on-message
Example Skeleton: [Headline]: [Brand] makes [promise]. Pillar 1: [proof A]. Pillar 2: [proof B]. Foundation: [mission]
Strengths: Scalable; easy to QA comms against; good for large orgs
Risks: Can become bureaucratic; pillars may feel disconnected

Purpose: Articulate a brand from functional to emotional to essence
Structure: Root strengths + Benefits (functional/emotional) + Discriminator + Values + Personality + Essence
Example Skeleton: Root: [quality ingredient]. Functional: [lasts longer]. Emotional: [confidence]. Essence: [be unstoppable]
Strengths: Holistic view from product to soul; widely understood
Risks: Essence can be vague; pyramid hides tensions

Purpose: Lead with purpose to inspire loyalty
When to Use: Purpose-driven brand strategy or culture alignment
Example Skeleton: Why: [We believe X]. How: [We do Y differently]. What: [Our product is Z]
Strengths: Memorable; emotionally resonant; great for culture decks
Risks: Hard to operationalize; WHY can feel generic

Purpose: Cast customer as hero to clarify brand narrative
Structure: Hero / Problem (external-internal-philosophical) / Guide / Plan / Call to action / Success / Failure
When to Use: Website copy; campaign messaging; sales narratives
Example Skeleton: [Customer] wants [goal] but faces [problem]. [Brand] as guide offers [plan]. Result: [success] vs [failure]
Strengths: Customer-centric; drives conversion; clear CTA structure
Risks: Overused; can oversimplify complex B2B sales

Purpose: Frame value around the functional or social job a customer hires the product for
Structure: Job statement + Struggling moment + Desired outcome + Competing solution
When to Use: Innovation briefs; ad copy rooted in usage context
Example Skeleton: When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome], instead of [alternative]
Strengths: Avoids feature-speak; grounded in real behavior
Risks: Requires deep customer interviews to get right

Purpose: Connect product specs to emotional value step by step
Structure: Feature -> Functional Benefit -> Emotional Benefit -> Value/Identity
Example Skeleton: Feature: [256GB storage]. Benefit: [store everything]. Emotional: [never delete a memory]. Value: [you are organized]
Risks: Risk of shallow laddering; emotional end may ring false

Purpose: Capture brand essence in a single memorable phrase
Structure: Core concept (distilled) + Verbal hook + Rhythm or sound
When to Use: Brand identity; campaign anchor; awareness advertising
Example Skeleton: [Brand] - [short punchy phrase that captures the essence], e.g. 'Do more. Worry less.'
Strengths: Iconic if done well; highly portable across channels
Risks: Hard to create; risks being generic or dated quickly

Purpose: Explain a brand or product in under 60 seconds to any audience
Structure: Hook + What it is + Who it's for + Key benefit + Call to action
When to Use: Speed networking; investor meetings; sales openers; onboarding new hires
Example Skeleton: We built [product] for [audience] who [need]. It [key benefit] so you can [outcome]. Want to [CTA]?
Strengths: Versatile; forces brevity; tests clarity of core message
Risks: Can feel rushed; hard to adapt for different audiences

Purpose: State a brand's beliefs and rallying cry in long-form prose
Structure: Belief statements + Enemy (what we fight against) + Community invitation + Future vision
When to Use: Brand launch; culture alignment; PR and content marketing
Example Skeleton: [Brand] believes [belief]. The world needs [change]. We fight [enemy]. Join us [CTA].
Strengths: Inspiring internally and externally; earns media attention
Risks: Easy to make grandiose; must be authentic to survive scrutiny

Purpose: Anchor claims on verifiable evidence to build credibility
Structure: 3-5 Messaging Pillars (claims) + Supporting Proof Points (data/stories/testimonials) per pillar
When to Use: Analyst relations; enterprise sales; thought leadership
Example Skeleton: Pillar: [We are the most reliable]. Proof 1: [99.99% uptime SLA]. Proof 2: [G2 leader 2024]. Proof 3: [case study].
Strengths: Credible and audit-able; reduces buyer risk
Risks: Proof can become stale; over-reliance on data dulls emotion
